content: Preoperative anaemia is a common condition, affecting between 5% and 76% of patients undergoing surgery. It is associated with an increased risk of requiring perioperative allogeneic blood transfusions, prolonged hospital stays, and higher rates of morbidity and mortality. One of the most frequent causes of anaemia is iron deficiency. Both oral and intravenous iron therapies are available as treatment options. Intravenous iron has been shown to be more effective in rapidly correcting iron stores in conditions such as inflammatory bowel disease, chronic heart failure, and postpartum haemorrhage. However, there is limited research specifically investigating the use of iron therapy for preoperative anaemia. The objective of this Cochrane Review was to evaluate the effects of preoperative iron therapy, whether administered orally or intravenously, on reducing the need for allogeneic blood transfusions in anaemic patients undergoing surgery. The review included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) that compared preoperative iron monotherapy to placebo, no treatment, standard care, or another form of iron therapy in adults with anaemia. Anaemia was defined as haemoglobin levels below 13 g/dL in males and below 12 g/dL in non-pregnant females. The search for relevant studies was conducted on July 30, 2018, and updated on November 28, 2019. Databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, Embase, and others were searched, along with clinical trial registries and reference lists. Six RCTs involving a total of 372 participants were included in the analysis. Four studies compared iron therapy (oral or intravenous) with no treatment, placebo, or standard care, while two studies compared intravenous iron therapy with oral iron therapy. The duration of iron therapy varied from 48 hours to three weeks before surgery. The meta-analysis revealed no significant difference in the proportion of participants requiring allogeneic blood transfusions between those who received iron therapy and those who received placebo or standard care (risk ratio [RR] 1.21, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.87 to 1.70; moderate-quality evidence). Similarly, a single study comparing oral and intravenous iron therapy found no difference in the risk of transfusion between the two groups. Preoperative haemoglobin levels at the end of the intervention did not differ significantly between the iron therapy and placebo/standard care groups (mean difference [MD] 0.63 g/dL, 95% CI -0.07 to 1.34; low-quality evidence). However, intravenous iron therapy resulted in a greater increase in haemoglobin levels compared to oral iron therapy (MD 1.23 g/dL, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.65; low-quality evidence). Ferritin levels were also significantly higher with intravenous iron therapy compared to standard care (MD 149.00 ng/mL, 95% CI 25.84 to 272.16; low-quality evidence) and oral iron therapy (MD 395.03 ng/mL, 95% CI 227.72 to 562.35; low-quality evidence). Not all studies assessed outcomes such as quality of life, short-term mortality, or postoperative morbidity. Some studies measured these outcomes but did not report the data, and those that did report the data were underpowered to draw definitive conclusions. As a result, uncertainty remains regarding these outcomes. The authors concluded that preoperative iron therapy does not significantly reduce the proportion of patients requiring allogeneic blood transfusions compared to no iron therapy. Intravenous iron therapy appears to result in greater increases in haemoglobin and ferritin levels compared to oral iron therapy, but the evidence is not robust. These conclusions are based on six studies, three of which had very small sample sizes. Further well-designed and adequately powered RCTs are needed to determine the true effectiveness of iron therapy for preoperative anaemia. Two ongoing studies, involving a total of 1500 participants, may provide more definitive evidence in the future.
